docs.title: Lab Manual: Setting Up a Splunk Cluster on a Single Docker Node
Introduction
docs.text: This lab demonstrates how to configure a Splunk cluster on a single Docker node. The setup includes the following components: - Master Node: Manages the cluster configuration. - Peer Node: Handles data indexing and replication. - Search Head: Provides the search interface for querying indexed data. - Application Container: Generates logs to be sent to Splunk for analysis.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Software Requirements:
  2. Install Docker: Docker Installation Guide.

  3. Install Docker Compose: Docker Compose Installation Guide.

  4. Hardware Requirements:

  5. Minimum 8 GB of RAM.
  6. At least 2 CPUs.
  7. Sufficient disk space for Splunk data.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Docker Compose File
docs.text:
1. Set up the working directory: 

    mkdir splunk-cluster && cd splunk-cluster

  2. Create the docker-compose.yml file: 

    nano docker-compose.yml

  3. Add the following content: 

    version: '3.8'

services:
  master:
    image: splunk/splunk
    container_name: splunk_master
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"   # Web interface for Master Node
      - "8089:8089"   # Management port
      - "9997:9997"   # Data forwarding port
    environment:
      - SPLUNK_START_ARGS=--accept-license
      - SPLUNK_PASSWORD=YourSecurePassword
    networks:
      - splunk-net

  peer:
    image: splunk/splunk
    container_name: splunk_peer
    ports:
      - "8001:8000"   # Web interface for Peer Node
      - "8088:8088"   # HTTP Event Collector port
      - "9998:9997"   # Replication port for Peer Node
    environment:
      - SPLUNK_START_ARGS=--accept-license
      - SPLUNK_PASSWORD=YourSecurePassword
    networks:
      - splunk-net

  search-head:
    image: splunk/splunk
    container_name: splunk_search_head
    ports:
      - "8002:8000"   # Web interface for Search Head
    environment:
      - SPLUNK_START_ARGS=--accept-license
      - SPLUNK_PASSWORD=YourSecurePassword
    networks:
      - splunk-net

networks:
  splunk-net:
    driver: bridge

  4. Save and close the file.

docs.title: Step 2: Deploy the Containers
docs.text:
1. Start all the containers: 

    docker-compose up -d

  2. Verify running containers: 

    docker ps
    You should see splunk_master, splunk_peer, and splunk_search_head running.

docs.title: Master Node Configuration
docs.text:
1. Open the Master Node interface: http://<your-node-ip>:8000.
  2. Log in with:
  3. Username: admin
  4. Password: YourSecurePassword.
  5. Navigate to Settings > Indexer Clustering.
  6. Click Enable Clustering and choose the role as Master Node.
  7. Configure:
  8. Replication Factor: 1 (for simplicity).
  9. Search Factor: 1 (for simplicity).
  10. Save the settings and restart the container when prompted.

docs.title: Peer Node Configuration
docs.text:
1. Open the Peer Node interface: http://<your-node-ip>:8001.
  2. Log in with the same credentials as the Master Node.
  3. Navigate to Settings > Indexer Clustering.
  4. Click Enable Clustering and choose the role as Peer Node.
  5. Enter the Master URI: https://splunk_master:8089.
  6. Configure:
  7. Replication Port: 9997.
  8. Use the same security key as the Master Node.
  9. Save the settings and restart the container.

docs.title: Search Head Configuration
docs.text:
1. Open the Search Head interface: http://<your-node-ip>:8002.
  2. Log in with the same credentials as the Master Node.
  3. Navigate to Settings > Indexer Clustering.
  4. Click Enable Clustering and choose the role as Search Head.
  5. Enter the Master URI: https://splunk_master:8089.
  6. Save the settings and restart the container.

docs.title: Step 4: Configure an Index
docs.text:
1. Open the Peer Node interface: http://<your-node-ip>:8001.
  2. Navigate to Settings > Indexes.
  3. Click New Index and configure:
  4. Index Name: tutorial_index.
  5. Use default settings for simplicity.
  6. Save the new index.

docs.title: Step 5: Set Up the HTTP Event Collector (HEC)
docs.text:
The HTTP Event Collector (HEC) allows applications and services to send data directly to Splunk.

  1. Access the Peer Node: Open http://<your-node-ip>:8001 in a browser and log in.

  2. Navigate to HEC Settings:

  3. Go to Settings > Data Inputs > HTTP Event Collector.

  4. Click Add New to create a new HEC.

  5. Create the HEC:

  6. Name: Enter a name like docker_logs_collector.
  7. Index: Select tutorial_index (created in Step 4).

  8. Click Next and then Submit.

  9. Retrieve the Token:

  10. After submission, a page with the generated token will appear.

  11. Copy the token value; this is your Your-HEC-Token.

  12. Enable the HEC:

  13. Go back to Settings > Data Inputs > HTTP Event Collector.
  14. Click Global Settings.
  15. Enable the HEC and choose All Tokens under "Allowed Indexes."
  16. Save the changes.

docs.title: Step 6: Send Logs from an Application Container
docs.text:
Use the Nginx container to generate logs and send them to Splunk via the HEC.

  1. Run the Nginx Container: Use the following command to start the Nginx container, replacing <Your-HEC-Token> with the token from Step 5 and <peer-node-ip> with the IP of the Peer Node: 
    docker run -p 80:80 \
--log-driver=splunk \
--log-opt splunk-token=<Your-HEC-Token> \
--log-opt splunk-url=https://<peer-node-ip>:8088 \
--log-opt splunk-insecureskipverify=true \
nginx

Explanation of the command: - The --log-driver=splunk sets Splunk as the logging driver. - --log-opt splunk-token=<Your-HEC-Token> uses the token for authentication with Splunk. - --log-opt splunk-url=https://<peer-node-ip>:8088 specifies the Peer Node as the log collector. - --log-opt splunk-insecureskipverify=true skips SSL certificate verification for simplicity.

  1. Access the Nginx Application:
  2. Open a browser and go to http://<your-node-ip>:80.

  3. Perform actions (e.g., refresh the page) to generate logs.

  4. Verify Logs in Splunk:

  5. Open the Search Head at http://<your-node-ip>:8002.
  6. Navigate to Search & Reporting.
  7. Query for logs: 
    index="tutorial_index"
  8. Check for Nginx logs to confirm the setup.

docs.title: Ports Used
docs.text: Port Description 8000 Web interface for Splunk components 8089 Management port for internal communication 9997 Data forwarding from universal forwarders 8088 HTTP Event Collector for receiving logs 80 Default web server port for testing (e.g., Nginx)

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
You have successfully set up a Splunk cluster on a single Docker node. Use this setup to explore Splunk's capabilities for log analysis and monitoring. You can expand this configuration by adding more nodes or integrating additional data sources.

Happy Splunking!

docs.title: Configuring Slack Alerts for Your Monitoring Lab
Introduction
docs.text:
This guide will walk you through setting up Slack alerts for your monitoring environment. By the end of this guide, you'll have your own Slack workspace with a dedicated channel for receiving monitoring alerts from both Zabbix and Grafana.

Time allocation: 15 minutes

docs.title: 1. Creating Your Own Slack Workspace
docs.text:
First, let's create your personal Slack workspace:

  1. Open your browser and go to slack.com/create

  2. Sign in with your Google account:

  3. Click "Continue with Google"
  4. Select your Google account

  5. Authorize Slack to access your account

  6. Enter your name and create a workspace:

  7. Enter your full name
  8. Name your workspace: YourName-Monitoring-Lab (replace YourName with your actual name)

  9. Skip the team invitation step (click "Skip for now")

  10. You now have your own Slack workspace!

docs.title: 2. Creating a Monitoring Alerts Channel
docs.text:
Next, create a dedicated channel for your monitoring alerts:

  1. In the left sidebar of Slack, click the "+" icon next to "Channels"

  2. Click "Create a channel"

  3. Enter the following details:

  4. Channel name: monitoring-alerts
  5. Description: Channel for receiving monitoring alerts from Zabbix and Grafana
  6. Make private: Leave unchecked

  7. Click "Create"

  8. Your new channel is now ready to receive alerts

docs.title: 3. Setting Up an Incoming Webhook
docs.text:
Now, create a webhook that will allow your monitoring tools to send messages to Slack:

  1. Go to api.slack.com/apps

  2. Click "Create New App"

  3. Choose "From scratch"
  4. Name your app "Monitoring Alerts"
  5. Select your newly created workspace from the dropdown

  6. Click "Create App"

  7. In the left sidebar, click on "Incoming Webhooks"

  8. Toggle the switch to "On" to activate incoming webhooks

  9. Scroll down and click "Add New Webhook to Workspace"

  10. Select the #monitoring-alerts channel you created earlier

  11. Click "Allow"

  12. You'll now see your webhook URL. Click "Copy" to copy it to your clipboard

  13. ⚠️ Important: Save this webhook URL securely - you'll need it for configuring both Zabbix and Grafana

docs.title: 4. Configuring Zabbix to Send Alerts to Slack
docs.text: Now, set up Zabbix to send alerts to your Slack channel:

docs.title: 4.1 Create a Slack Media Type in Zabbix
docs.text:
1. Log in to your Zabbix web interface

  2. Navigate to Administration → Media types

  3. Click Create media type (in the top-right corner)

  4. Configure the following settings:

  5. Name: Slack Alerts
  6. Type: Webhook

  7. Click "Add" in the Parameters section and add:

    • Name: webhook_url
    • Value: Paste your Slack webhook URL that you copied earlier

  8. In the Script field, paste the following code: 

    try {
    var params = JSON.parse(value);
    var req = new CurlHttpRequest();
    req.AddHeader('Content-Type: application/json');

    // Format timestamp
    var timestamp = params.event_date + ' ' + params.event_time;

    // Determine emoji based on severity
    var emoji = "🔵"; // Info default
    if (params.severity == "Warning") {
        emoji = "🟡";
    } else if (params.severity == "Average") {
        emoji = "🟠";
    } else if (params.severity == "High") {
        emoji = "🔴";
    } else if (params.severity == "Disaster") {
        emoji = "⚫";
    }

    var data = {
        "blocks": [
            {
                "type": "header",
                "text": {
                    "type": "plain_text",
                    "text": emoji + " " + params.event_status + ": " + params.trigger_name
                }
            },
            {
                "type": "section",
                "fields": [
                    {
                        "type": "mrkdwn",
                        "text": "*Host:*\n" + params.host_name
                    },
                    {
                        "type": "mrkdwn",
                        "text": "*Severity:*\n" + params.severity
                    },
                    {
                        "type": "mrkdwn",
                        "text": "*Time:*\n" + timestamp
                    },
                    {
                        "type": "mrkdwn",
                        "text": "*Event ID:*\n" + params.event_id
                    }
                ]
            },
            {
                "type": "section",
                "text": {
                    "type": "mrkdwn",
                    "text": "*Description:*\n" + params.trigger_description
                }
            }
        ]
    };

    var resp = req.Post(params.webhook_url, JSON.stringify(data));

    if (req.Status() != 200) {
        throw "Response code: " + req.Status();
    }

    return resp;
} catch (error) {
    return "Error: " + error;
}

  9. Click the Message templates tab

  10. Add the following templates:

  11. For Problem: Click "Add" and paste the following: 

    {
    "webhook_url": "{ALERT.SENDTO}",
    "event_status": "PROBLEM",
    "trigger_name": "{TRIGGER.NAME}",
    "trigger_description": "{TRIGGER.DESCRIPTION}",
    "host_name": "{HOST.NAME}",
    "severity": "{TRIGGER.SEVERITY}",
    "event_id": "{EVENT.ID}",
    "event_date": "{EVENT.DATE}",
    "event_time": "{EVENT.TIME}"
}

  12. For Recovery: Click "Add" and paste the following: 

    {
    "webhook_url": "{ALERT.SENDTO}",
    "event_status": "RESOLVED",
    "trigger_name": "{TRIGGER.NAME}",
    "trigger_description": "{TRIGGER.DESCRIPTION}",
    "host_name": "{HOST.NAME}",
    "severity": "{TRIGGER.SEVERITY}",
    "event_id": "{EVENT.ID}",
    "event_date": "{EVENT.DATE}",
    "event_time": "{EVENT.TIME}"
}

  13. Click Add at the bottom to save the media type

docs.title: 4.2 Set Up User Media
docs.text:
Now, configure how you'll receive these Slack notifications:

  1. Go to Administration → Users

  2. Click on your username (e.g., Admin)

  3. Switch to the Media tab

  4. Click Add

  5. Enter:

  6. Type: Slack Alerts (select from dropdown)
  7. Send to: Paste your webhook URL
  8. When active: Leave as default (1-7,00:00-24:00)
  9. Use if severity: Check all severities you want to receive

  10. Enabled: Checked

  11. Click Add to save the media

  12. Click Update to save the user configuration

docs.title: 4.3 Create an Action
docs.text:
Finally, create an action that will send alerts when triggers activate:

  1. Go to Configuration → Actions

  2. Make sure "Trigger actions" is selected in the dropdown

  3. Click Create action

  4. In the Action tab:

  5. Name: Send to Slack
  6. Conditions: By default, this will fire for all triggers. You can add conditions to limit which triggers send alerts.

  7. Click "Add" under "New condition" if you want to add specific conditions (such as minimum severity)

  8. Switch to the Operations tab:

  9. Default operation step duration: 1h (this ensures you don't get flooded with alerts)

  10. Add an operation:

    • Operation type: Send message
    • Steps: 1-10 (will send for steps 1-10)
    • User groups: Select Administrators (or appropriate group)
    • Send to users: Select your username
    • Send only to: Slack Alerts

  11. Add a recovery operation:

  12. Operation type: Send message
  13. User groups: Select Administrators (or appropriate group)
  14. Send to users: Select your username

  15. Send only to: Slack Alerts

  16. Click Add at the bottom to create the action

docs.title: 5. Configuring Grafana to Send Alerts to Slack
docs.text:
Now, set up Grafana to also send alerts to your Slack channel:

  1. Log in to your Grafana web interface

  2. In the left sidebar, click on the gear icon (⚙️) to open the Configuration menu

  3. Select Notification channels

  4. Click Add channel

  5. Enter the following details:

  6. Name: Slack Alerts
  7. Type: Select Slack from the dropdown
  8. URL: Paste your Slack webhook URL
  9. Recipient: #monitoring-alerts
  10. Mention: Leave blank (or add @here if you want to be notified)
  11. Token: Leave blank (not needed with webhooks)
  12. Check "Include image" if you want graph images in alerts

  13. Default (send on all alerts): Check this box

  14. Click Send Test to verify your configuration works

  15. Check your Slack channel for the test message

  16. Click Save after confirming the test worked

docs.title: 6. Creating a Test Alert in Grafana
docs.text:
Let's create a simple test alert in Grafana:

  1. Navigate to one of your dashboards (e.g., System Monitoring Dashboard)

  2. Find a panel showing CPU usage and click on its title, then select Edit

  3. In the panel editor, click the Alert tab

  4. Click Create Alert

  5. Configure the alert:

  6. Name: Test Alert - High CPU Usage
  7. Evaluate every: 1m
  8. For: 5m (alert will trigger if condition is true for 5 minutes)
  9. Conditions:
    • WHEN: avg() of query(A, 5m, now)
    • IS ABOVE: 80

  10. No Data & Error Handling:

    • If no data or all values are null: No Data
    • If execution error: Alerting

  11. Under Notifications:

  12. Send to: Select Slack Alerts

  13. Message: Enter a custom message like: 

    This is a test alert for high CPU usage. This would indicate a real problem in production.

  14. Click Save in the upper right

docs.title: 7. Testing Your Alerts
docs.text: Let's verify both alerting systems are working:

docs.title: 7.1 Testing Zabbix Alerts
docs.text:
Generate some load to trigger a Zabbix alert:

docker-compose exec zabbix-agent stress --cpu 4 --timeout 120

docs.title: 7.2 Testing Grafana Alerts
docs.text: For Grafana alerts, you can either: - Wait for the CPU alert to trigger naturally (if CPU stays high) - Or temporarily lower the threshold in your Grafana alert to trigger it with normal load

docs.title: 7.3 Verify in Slack
docs.text: After running the tests: 1. Open your Slack workspace 2. Go to the #monitoring-alerts channel 3. Verify you received alerts from both systems 4. Check that the alert formatting looks correct and contains all necessary information

docs.title: 8.1 Testing Real-World Alert Scenarios
docs.text: Let's test your alerts with real-world scenarios:

docs.title: Scenario 1: Container Failure
docs.text:
Simulate a service going down by stopping a critical container:

# Stop the web application container
docker-compose stop web-app

# Wait 2-3 minutes for alerts to trigger
# Then restart the container
docker-compose start web-app

This should trigger alerts related to web service availability. In your Slack channel, you should see alerts about the web application being unreachable, followed by recovery notifications when you restart the container.

docs.title: Scenario 2: High System Load
docs.text:
Generate high CPU load to trigger resource alerts:

# Generate CPU load for 2 minutes
docker-compose exec zabbix-agent stress --cpu 4 --timeout 120

docs.title: Scenario 3: Database Connection Failure
docs.text:
Simulate database problems by stopping the MySQL service:

# Stop the MySQL container
docker-compose stop mysql-service

# Wait 2-3 minutes for alerts to trigger
# Then restart the container
docker-compose start mysql-service

This should trigger database connectivity alerts in both Zabbix and Grafana.

docs.title: 8.2 Troubleshooting Alert Issues
docs.text: If your alerts aren't working properly, here are some steps to diagnose and fix the problems:

docs.title: 8.1 Test Slack Webhook Directly
docs.text:
You can test if your Slack webhook is working correctly using a simple curl command:

curl -X POST -H 'Content-type: application/json' --data '{"text":"This is a test message from curl"}' YOUR_WEBHOOK_URL

Replace YOUR_WEBHOOK_URL with your actual Slack webhook URL. If successful, you should see a "ok" response and the message should appear in your Slack channel.

docs.title: 8.2 Check Zabbix Media Type Configuration
docs.text:
Verify your Zabbix Slack media type is set up correctly:

  1. In Zabbix, go to Administration → Media types
  2. Find your Slack media type and click Test
  3. Enter your webhook URL in the "Send to" field
  4. Add test values: 
    {
    "event_status": "TEST",
    "trigger_name": "Test Trigger",
    "trigger_description": "This is a test alert",
    "host_name": "Test Host",
    "severity": "High",
    "event_id": "12345",
    "event_date": "2025-03-12",
    "event_time": "15:45:00"
}
  5. Click Test to send a test message

If the test fails, check: - Your webhook URL for typos - That your script has no JavaScript errors - That your script has access to the CurlHttpRequest function

docs.title: 8.3 Check Zabbix Action Configuration
docs.text:
Verify your action is properly configured:

docker-compose exec zabbix-server zabbix_server -R config_cache_reload

Then check the Zabbix server logs for any errors:

docker-compose logs zabbix-server | grep -i error

docs.title: 8.4 Test Grafana Webhook
docs.text:
Check if Grafana can reach your Slack webhook:

  1. In Grafana, go to Alerting → Notification channels
  2. Find your Slack channel and click Test
  3. If it fails, check Grafana's logs: 
    docker-compose logs grafana | grep -i error

docs.title: 8.5 Check Network Connectivity
docs.text:
Make sure your containers can reach the Slack API:

docker-compose exec zabbix-server curl -I https://hooks.slack.com

You should see an HTTP/2 200 response. If not, there might be network connectivity issues.

docs.title: 8.6 Verify Trigger Conditions
docs.text:
If alerts aren't firing when you expect:

  1. Check if your triggers are actually being activated:
  2. In Zabbix, go to Monitoring → Problems

  3. In Grafana, go to Alerting → Alert Rules

  4. Make sure the conditions are being met:

  5. For CPU alerts, verify the load is actually high enough

  6. Check the time conditions (has it been in alert state long enough?)

  7. For Zabbix, you can manually check the current value: 

    docker-compose exec zabbix-server zabbix_get -s zabbix-agent -k system.cpu.util[,idle]
    This returns the idle CPU percentage - if it's below 20%, a CPU alert (80% usage) should trigger

docs.title: 8.7 Check Webhook Response Codes
docs.text:
If you suspect the webhook is receiving but not processing your alerts:

# For Zabbix
docker-compose exec zabbix-server tail -f /var/log/zabbix/zabbix_server.log | grep -i webhook

# For Grafana
docker-compose exec grafana tail -f /var/log/grafana/grafana.log | grep -i slack

Look for HTTP status codes in the logs - you want to see 200 responses.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
You've successfully set up Slack alerting for your monitoring lab! Your alerts will now be delivered to your dedicated Slack channel, making it easy to track and respond to monitoring events.

This integration demonstrates how modern monitoring systems can connect with communication tools to streamline incident response. In a production environment, you might extend this system with additional features like:

  • Different channels for different severity levels
  • Integration with incident management systems
  • Automated escalation procedures
  • Runbook links in alerts to guide troubleshooting

For this lab, your current setup provides a solid foundation for understanding how alerting works in a monitoring environment.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This guide walks you through creating a complete monitoring environment using Docker containers with Zabbix, Grafana, and Loki. You'll establish a self-contained environment for learning modern monitoring practices with secure communications between components.

Estimated Time: 45 minutes - Environment Preparation: 15 minutes - Certificate Generation: 10 minutes - Container Deployment: 20 minutes

Additional Resources: - Zabbix 6.0 Quick Installation Guide

docs.title: System Updates and Prerequisites
docs.text:
First, update your system and install the necessary prerequisites:

# Update package repositories
sudo apt-get update

# Install Docker dependencies
sudo apt-get install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl software-properties-common

docs.title: Docker Installation
docs.text:
Add Docker's repository and install Docker with Docker Compose:

# Add Docker's GPG key
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | sudo apt-key add -

# Add Docker repository
sudo add-apt-repository "deb [arch=amd64] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) stable"

# Update package database
sudo apt-get update

# Install Docker and Docker Compose
sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-compose

# Add your user to the docker group
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

# Apply group membership
newgrp docker

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Confirm Docker is properly installed:

# Check Docker version
docker --version

# Check Docker Compose version
docker-compose --version

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
Create the directory structure for the monitoring environment:

# Create main project directory
mkdir -p monitoring-lab

# Create subdirectories
mkdir -p monitoring-lab/certs
mkdir -p monitoring-lab/data/{mysql,mysql-service,promtail}
mkdir -p monitoring-lab/grafana/data
mkdir -p monitoring-lab/web-app
mkdir -p monitoring-lab/zabbix/{alertscripts,externalscripts}

# Navigate to project directory
cd monitoring-lab

Your project structure will look like this:

monitoring-lab/
├── certs/                  # SSL certificates
│   ├── ca.crt
│   ├── grafana.crt
│   ├── grafana.key
│   ├── zabbix-agent.crt
│   ├── zabbix-agent.key
│   ├── zabbix-server.crt
│   └── zabbix-server.key
├── data/
│   ├── mysql/              # Zabbix MySQL data
│   ├── mysql-service/      # Separate MySQL service data
│   └── promtail/
│       └── config.yml      # Promtail configuration
├── grafana/
│   └── data/               # Grafana persistent data
├── web-app/                # NGINX web app files
└── zabbix/
    ├── agent.conf          # Zabbix agent configuration
    ├── alertscripts/       # Zabbix alert scripts
    └── externalscripts/    # Zabbix external scripts

docs.title: Certificate Generation
docs.text: Generate self-signed certificates for secure communications between components:

docs.title: Certificate Authority
docs.text:
# Navigate to certs directory
cd certs

# Generate CA private key
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 4096

# Generate self-signed CA certificate
openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key ca.key -sha256 -days 365 -out ca.crt -subj "/CN=Monitoring Lab CA"

docs.title: Zabbix Server Certificate
docs.text:
# Generate Zabbix server private key
openssl genrsa -out zabbix-server.key 2048

# Create certificate signing request
openssl req -new -key zabbix-server.key -out zabbix-server.csr -subj "/CN=zabbix-server"

# Sign the certificate with your CA
openssl x509 -req -in zabbix-server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out zabbix-server.crt -days 365 -sha256

docs.title: Zabbix Agent Certificate
docs.text:
# Generate Zabbix agent private key
openssl genrsa -out zabbix-agent.key 2048

# Create certificate signing request
openssl req -new -key zabbix-agent.key -out zabbix-agent.csr -subj "/CN=zabbix-agent"

# Sign the certificate with your CA
openssl x509 -req -in zabbix-agent.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out zabbix-agent.crt -days 365 -sha256

docs.title: Grafana Certificate
docs.text:
# Generate Grafana private key
openssl genrsa -out grafana.key 2048

# Create certificate signing request
openssl req -new -key grafana.key -out grafana.csr -subj "/CN=grafana"

# Sign the certificate with your CA
openssl x509 -req -in grafana.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial -out grafana.crt -days 365 -sha256

docs.title: Certificate Permissions
docs.text:
# Set certificate permissions
chmod 644 *.crt ca.crt

# Set private key permissions
chmod 600 *.key ca.key

# Return to main directory
cd ..

docs.title: Zabbix Agent Configuration
docs.text:
Create a configuration file for the Zabbix agent:

# Create and edit Zabbix agent config file
nano zabbix/agent.conf

Paste the following configuration:

# Zabbix Agent 2 configuration
Server=zabbix-server
ServerActive=zabbix-server
Hostname=zabbix-agent

# TLS parameters
TLSConnect=cert
TLSAccept=cert
TLSCAFile=/etc/ssl/certs/ca.crt
TLSCertFile=/etc/ssl/certs/zabbix-agent.crt
TLSKeyFile=/etc/ssl/private/zabbix-agent.key

# Enable remote commands
EnableRemoteCommands=1
LogRemoteCommands=1

# Enable Docker monitoring
Plugins.Docker.Endpoint=unix:///var/run/docker.sock

# Monitor host filesystem
HostMetadata=linux
HostInterface=0.0.0.0

docs.title: Promtail Configuration
docs.text:
Create a configuration file for Promtail (log collector):

# Create and edit Promtail config file
nano data/promtail/config.yml

Paste the following configuration:

server:
  http_listen_port: 9080
  grpc_listen_port: 0

positions:
  filename: /etc/promtail/positions.yaml

clients:
  - url: http://loki:3100/loki/api/v1/push

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: system
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - localhost
        labels:
          job: varlogs
          __path__: /var/log/*.log

  - job_name: docker
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - localhost
        labels:
          job: docker
          __path__: /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*.log

docs.title: Sample Web Application
docs.text:
Create a sample web page to monitor:

# Create and edit sample web page
nano web-app/index.html

Paste the following HTML:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Monitoring Lab Sample Web App</title>
    <style>
        body {
            font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
            margin: 40px;
            line-height: 1.6;
        }
        h1 {
            color: #333;
        }
        .status {
            padding: 20px;
            background-color: #f9f9f9;
            border-radius: 5px;
            border: 1px solid #ddd;
            margin-top: 20px;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Monitoring Lab Sample Web Application</h1>
    <p>This is a sample web application for monitoring with Zabbix.</p>
    <div class="status">
        <h2>Server Status</h2>
        <p>Server Time: <span id="server-time"></span></p>
        <p>Status: <span style="color: green; font-weight: bold;">ONLINE</span></p>
    </div>
    <script>
        function updateTime() {
            document.getElementById("server-time").textContent = new Date().toLocaleString();
        }
        updateTime();
        setInterval(updateTime, 1000);
    </script>
</body>
</html>

docs.title: Set Permissions
docs.text:
Set appropriate permissions for Grafana data and verify your certificates:

# Set Grafana data directory permissions
sudo chown -R 472:472 grafana/data

# Verify SSL certificates
ls -la certs/
chmod 644 certs/*.crt
chmod 600 certs/*.key

docs.title: Docker Compose Configuration
docs.text:
Create a Docker Compose file to define all services:

# Create docker-compose.yml
nano docker-compose.yml

For Docker Compose configuration, see the separate docker-compose.yml file in your project repository.

docs.title: Start Services
docs.text:
Launch all the containers:

# Start all containers
docker-compose up -d

This process may take several minutes as Docker downloads the necessary images.

docs.title: Verify Deployment
docs.text:
Check that all services are running:

# Check container status
docker-compose ps

If any container shows a status other than "Up" or "(healthy)", check its logs:

# Check logs of a specific container
docker-compose logs [container-name]

docs.title: Database Configuration
docs.text:
Set up a test database for monitoring:

# Configure the test database
docker-compose exec mysql-service mysql -u root -pmysql_pwd -e "
USE testdb;

CREATE TABLE test_data (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  value DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  timestamp TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

INSERT INTO test_data (name, value) VALUES 
  ('Server CPU', 45.5),
  ('Server Memory', 78.2),
  ('Database Connections', 125),
  ('Active Users', 1250),
  ('Response Time', 0.85);

CREATE USER 'monitor'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'monitor_pwd';
GRANT SELECT, PROCESS, SHOW DATABASES, REPLICATION CLIENT ON *.* TO 'monitor'@'%';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;"

Note: Replace mysql_pwd and monitor_pwd with secure passwords.

docs.title: Accessing Services
docs.text:
Access your monitoring services through a web browser:

  • Zabbix Web Interface
  • URL: https://your-server-ip:8443
  • Username: Admin

  • Password: zabbix

  • Grafana Web Interface

  • URL: http://your-server-ip:3000
  • Username: admin

  • Password: admin

  • Sample Web Application

  • URL: http://your-server-ip:8080

Note: Since you're using self-signed certificates, your browser will show a security warning. For this lab environment, you can safely proceed by accepting the risk.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The monitoring environment consists of several interconnected components:

  1. Zabbix Server: Central monitoring system that collects and processes metrics
  2. Zabbix Agent: Collects local system metrics from monitored hosts
  3. Grafana: Visualization platform for metrics and dashboards
  4. Loki: Log aggregation system that collects and indexes logs
  5. Promtail: Log collection agent that forwards logs to Loki
  6. MySQL: Database storage for Zabbix and service metrics

The components are secured using self-signed certificates and communicate over an isolated Docker network.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If you encounter issues during setup:

# If Docker gives permission errors
newgrp docker

# Check container logs
docker-compose logs [container-name]

# Access a container's shell
docker-compose exec [container-name] bash

# Fix volume permissions if needed
sudo chown -R 1000:1000 ./data
sudo chmod -R 755 ./data

docs.title: Advanced Configuration
docs.text:
After completing the basic setup, consider these advanced configurations:

  • Create custom Zabbix triggers and notifications
  • Build Grafana dashboards to visualize metrics
  • Configure alert thresholds for key metrics
  • Add additional services to monitor
  • Set up notification channels (email, Slack, etc.)

docs.title: Lab Overview
docs.text:
In this lab, you will configure the Zabbix 7.0 monitoring system that was deployed in Lab 1. You'll set up comprehensive monitoring for system resources, web applications, and databases, leveraging Zabbix 7.0's advanced features.

Lab Time: 1 hour

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Completed Lab 1 with all containers running
  • Basic understanding of monitoring concepts
  • Access to the Zabbix web interface

docs.title: Lab Tasks
docs.text:
1. Configure Zabbix initial settings
  2. Set up system monitoring
  3. Configure web application monitoring
  4. Implement database monitoring
  5. Explore Zabbix 7.0 specific features

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
1. Access Zabbix at https://your-server-ip:8443 (credentials: Admin/zabbix)
  2. Change default admin password via Profile settings
  3. Configure UI: Administration → General → GUI
  4. Set Dark theme and working hours (09:00-18:00)

docs.title: User Management
docs.text:
1. Create Administrator group:
  2. Path: Administration → User groups

  3. Permissions: Grant full system access

  4. Create admin user:

  5. Path: Administration → Users
  6. Assign Admin role and add to Administrators group
  7. Use strong password with complexity requirements

docs.title: Host Configuration
docs.text:
1. Get agent IP: docker inspect zabbix-agent | grep IPAddress

Critical requirement: Set host names EXACTLY matching container names

  1. Configure Host Monitoring:

#### Zabbix Server Host - Navigate to Data Collection → Hosts → zabbix-server - Update the Interface field with the correct Agent IP: [Agent IP]:10050 - Templates are already applied - no need to modify

#### Zabbix Agent Host - Navigate to Data Collection → Hosts → Create host - Host name: zabbix-agent (must match container name exactly) - Interface: [Agent IP]:10050 - Template: "Linux by Zabbix agent active" - Configure certificate-based security: - Host connections: Certificate - From host: Both "No encryption" and "Certificate" - Set TLSConnect=cert and TLSAccept=cert

#### MySQL Service Host - Navigate to Data Collection → Hosts → Create host - Configure: - Host name: mysql-service - Interface: [Agent IP]:10050 - Templates: MySQL by Zabbix agent 2 - Macros: - {$MYSQL.DSN}: tcp://mysql-service:3306 - {$MYSQL.USER}: monitor - {$MYSQL.PASSWORD}: monitor_pwd - Click Add

  1. Verify Host Connectivity:
  2. Navigate to Monitoring → Problems
  3. Wait a few minutes for connections to establish
  4. Check Monitoring → Latest data for incoming metrics

docs.title: Task 3: Web Application Monitoring
docs.text:
Check the documentation for web monitoring in Zabbix:

https://www.zabbix.com/documentation/current/en/manual/web_monitoring

  1. Configure a Web Monitoring Host:
  2. Navigate to Monitoring → Hosts → Create host
  3. Configure:
    • Host name: web-app
    • Interface: [Agent IP]:10050
    • Templates: Website by Browser, Website certificate by Zabbix agent 2

  4. Click Add

  5. Create a Web Scenario:

  6. Go to the web-app host → Web tab
  7. Click Create web scenario
  8. Name: Web App Availability
  9. Application: Web monitoring
  10. Agent: Zabbix
  11. Steps:
    • Step name: Homepage
    • URL: http://your-server-ip:8080/
    • Required status codes: 200
    • Follow redirects: Yes

  12. Click Add

  13. Check Web Monitoring Results:

  14. Wait a few minutes for data collection
  15. Navigate to Monitoring → Latest data
  16. Filter by host: web-app
  17. Verify web monitoring metrics are being collected

Press couple times to Web Test page, metrics will start running

docs.title: Task 4: Database Monitoring
docs.text:
Check the documentation for dashboard in Zabbix:

https://www.zabbix.com/documentation/7.2/en/manual/web_interface/frontend_sections/dashboards?hl=Dashboard%2Cdashboard

Repo for Mysql: https://github.com/zabbix/zabbix/tree/master/templates/db/mysql_agent

  1. Verify MySQL Monitoring:
  2. Navigate to Monitoring → Latest data
  3. Filter by host: mysql-service

  4. Review the MySQL metrics being collected

  5. Create a MySQL Performance Dashboard:

  6. Navigate to Dashboards-> All Dashboards
  7. Click Create dashboard
  8. Name: MySQL Performance
  9. Add a Graph widget:
    • Title: MySQL Connections
    • Data source: Time series
    • Add you mysql-service as data co
  10. Add additional widgets for:
    • MySQL Query Rate
    • MySQL Buffer Pool Usage
    • MySQL Slow Queries

  11. Click Apply to save

  12. Try to add a Custom SQL Query:

Some instructions here: https://sbcode.net/zabbix/setup_mysql_database_monitoring/

  • If you change some configs in Docker, don't forget to restart the container.
  • We already have monitoring for the user.
  • Refer to the section about template_db_mysql.conf for more details.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If you encounter issues during this lab:

docs.title: Host Connection Problems:
docs.text:
• Verify the agent IP address is correct
  • Check that hostnames match exactly between Zabbix and agent config
  • Temporarily disable encryption to test connectivity
  • Review logs: docker logs zabbix-agent or docker logs zabbix-server

docs.title: No Data Collection:
docs.text:
• Verify templates are properly linked
  • Check item configuration details
  • Ensure the agent can access the services it's monitoring
  • Check for network connectivity between containers

docs.title: MySQL Monitoring Issues:
docs.text:
• Verify the monitor user exists: SELECT User FROM mysql.user WHERE User='monitor';
  • Check permissions: SHOW GRANTS FOR 'monitor'@'%';
  • Confirm DSN and credential macros are correct
  • Test MySQL connectivity

docs.title: Monitooringu Labor 3 - Grafana ja Loki seadistamine
Sissejuhatus
docs.text: Selles labori viimases osas seadistate Grafana visualiseerimissüsteemi ja Loki logikogumise lahenduse.

docs.title: 1. Docker Compose faili täiendamine
docs.text: Enne labori alustamist on vaja kontrollida ja täiendada Docker Compose faili, et kõik teenused oleksid õigesti seadistatud.

docs.title: 1.1 Loki teenuse täiendamine
docs.text:
Avage Docker Compose fail: 

nano docker-compose.yml

Leidke Loki teenuse konfiguratsioon ja lisage puuduv volume: 

loki:
  image: grafana/loki:2.7.3
  container_name: loki
  command: -config.file=/etc/loki/local-config.yaml
  ports:
    - "3100:3100"
  volumes:
    - ./data/loki:/etc/loki  # LISA SEE RIDA!
  restart: unless-stopped
  networks:
    - monitoring-network

docs.title: 1.2 Promtail teenuse täiendamine
docs.text:
Leidke Promtail teenuse konfiguratsioon ja lisage puuduv volume: 

promtail:
  image: grafana/promtail:2.7.3
  container_name: promtail
  volumes:
    - /var/log:/var/log
    - ./data/promtail:/etc/promtail
    - /var/lib/docker/containers:/var/lib/docker/containers:ro  # LISA SEE RIDA!
    # Docker socketi volume on juba olemas, mis on hea
  command: -config.file=/etc/promtail/config.yml
  depends_on:
    - loki
  restart: unless-stopped
  networks:
    - monitoring-network

docs.title: 1.3 Rakenda muudatused
docs.text:
Salvestage muudatused ja taaskäivitage teenused: 

docker-compose down loki promtail
docker-compose up -d loki promtail

docs.title: 2.1 Loo vajalikud kataloogid
docs.text:
mkdir -p ./data/loki
mkdir -p ./data/promtail

docs.title: 2.2 Loo Loki konfiguratsioonifail
docs.text:
nano ./data/loki/local-config.yaml

Kopeeri sinna järgmine sisu: 

auth_enabled: false

server:
  http_listen_port: 3100

ingester:
  lifecycler:
    address: 127.0.0.1
    ring:
      kvstore:
        store: inmemory
      replication_factor: 1
    final_sleep: 0s
  chunk_idle_period: 5m
  chunk_retain_period: 30s

schema_config:
  configs:
    - from: 2020-10-24
      store: boltdb-shipper
      object_store: filesystem
      schema: v11
      index:
        prefix: index_
        period: 24h

storage_config:
  boltdb_shipper:
    active_index_directory: /tmp/loki/boltdb-shipper-active
    cache_location: /tmp/loki/boltdb-shipper-cache
    cache_ttl: 24h
    shared_store: filesystem
  filesystem:
    directory: /tmp/loki/chunks

limits_config:
  enforce_metric_name: false
  reject_old_samples: true
  reject_old_samples_max_age: 168h

docs.title: 2.3 Loo Promtail konfiguratsioonifail
docs.text:
nano ./data/promtail/config.yml

Kopeeri sinna järgmine sisu: 

server:
  http_listen_port: 9080
  grpc_listen_port: 0

positions:
  filename: /etc/promtail/positions.yaml

clients:
  - url: http://loki:3100/loki/api/v1/push

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: system
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - localhost
        labels:
          job: varlogs
          __path__: /var/log/*.log

  - job_name: containers
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - localhost
        labels:
          job: containerlogs
          __path__: /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*.log

  - job_name: zabbix
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - localhost
        labels:
          job: zabbix
          __path__: /var/log/zabbix/*.log

  - job_name: nginx
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - localhost
        labels:
          job: nginx
          __path__: /var/log/nginx/*.log

  - job_name: mysql
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - localhost
        labels:
          job: mysql
          __path__: /var/log/mysql/*.log

  # Docker konteineri logide jälgimine
  - job_name: docker
    docker_sd_configs:
      - host: unix:///var/run/docker.sock
        refresh_interval: 5s
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: ['__meta_docker_container_name']
        regex: '/(.*)'
        target_label: 'container'

docs.title: 2.4 Taaskäivita Loki ja Promtail teenused
docs.text: docker-compose restart loki promtail

docs.title: 2.5 Kontrolli, et teenused töötavad
docs.text:
docker-compose ps loki promtail
docker-compose logs loki | tail
docker-compose logs promtail | tail

docs.title: 3.1 Ligipääs Grafana veebiliidesele
docs.text:
1. Ava veebibrauser ja navigeeri URL-ile: 

    http://your-server-ip:3000

  2. Logi sisse vaikimisi kasutajanime ja parooliga:

  3. Kasutajanimi: admin

  4. Parool: admin

  5. Kui sul palutakse parooli muuta, sisesta uus turvaline parool ja kliki Submit.

docs.title: 3.2 Lisa Loki andmeallikas
docs.text:
1. Navigeeri Configuration → Data Sources vasakul menüüs.

  2. Kliki Add data source.

  3. Otsi ja vali "Loki" nimekirjast.

  4. Sisesta järgmised seaded:

  5. Name: Loki
  6. URL: http://loki:3100

  7. Access: Server (default)

  8. Kliki Save & Test.

Peaksid nägema rohelist teadet, mis kinnitab edukat ühendust Lokiga.

docs.title: 3.3 Logide vaatamine Lokis
docs.text:
1. Kliki Explore ikoonil (kompass) vasakul menüüs.

  2. Vali Loki andmeallikate rippmenüüst lehe ülaosas.

  3. Sisesta lihtne päring logide nägemiseks: 

    {job="varlogs"}

  4. Klikki Run query logide nägemiseks.

  5. Docker konteineri logide jaoks kasuta: 

    {job="docker"}

  6. Otsinguid saad täpsustada lisades teksti otsingutingimusi: 

    {job="docker"} |= "error"
    See näitab ainult Docker logisid, mis sisaldavad sõna "error".

  7. Kasuta ajavahemiku valijat üleval paremal, et kohandada, millise perioodi logisid kuvatakse.

Märkus: Võib kuluda mõni minut, enne kui Promtail kogub logisid ja saadab need Lokisse. Kui te logisid kohe ei näe, oodake mõni minut ja proovige uuesti.

docs.title: 3.4 Lisa Zabbix andmeallikas
docs.text:
Kui sa ei leia Zabbix andmeallikat, siis installi see: 

docker exec -it grafana sh
docker exec -it grafana grafana-cli plugins install alexanderzobnin-zabbix-app
docker ps | grep grafana
docker-compose restart grafana

Seejärel seadista Zabbix andmeallikas: - Konfigureeri Zabbix andmeallikas: URL väljale: http://zabbix-web:8080/api_jsonrpc.php - Kasutajanimi: Admin - Parool: zabbix

Võib-olla pead lisama ka MySQL andmeallika (ZabbixDB)

Configuration → Data Sources
Click "Add data source"
Select "MySQL" as the data source type
Configure the MySQL connection:

Name: ZabbixDB (või mis tahes nimi, mida eelistad)
Host: zabbix-mysql
Database: zabbix
User: zabbix
Password: zabbix_pwd

Click "Save & Test" to verify the connection works

docs.title: 4. Esimese logidashboardi loomine
docs.text:
Loome lihtsa dashboardi logide jälgimiseks:

  1. Navigeeri vasakult menüüst Dashboards → + New Dashboard.

  2. Kliki Add visualization.

  3. Päringueditoris vali andmeallikaks Loki.

  4. Lisa teine paneel süsteemi logidega, klikkides uuesti Add panel ja kasutades päringut: 

    {job="varlogs"}

  5. Salvesta dashboard klikkides kettaikooni üleval paremal ja anna talle nimi, nt "System Monitoring".

docs.title: 5. Testlogide genereerimine
docs.text:
Genereerime mõned testilogid, et neid oleks võimalik visualiseerida:

  1. Genereeri süsteemi logid: 

    docker-compose exec zabbix-agent bash -c 'for i in {1..20}; do logger "INFO: System check completed successfully at $(date)"; sleep 1; done'

  2. Genereeri vealogid: 

    docker-compose exec zabbix-agent bash -c 'for i in {1..5}; do logger "ERROR: Database connection timeout at $(date)"; sleep 1; done'

  3. Genereeri veebiseveri logid, tehes HTTP päringuid: 

    for i in {1..10}; do curl http://localhost:8080/ >/dev/null 2>&1; curl http://localhost:8080/login.php >/dev/null 2>&1; sleep 1; done

docs.title: 6. Logi analüüsi dashboardi loomine Grafanas
docs.text:
Loome dashboardi logide analüüsimiseks:

  1. Navigeeri Dashboards → New Dashboard.

  2. Kliki Add new panel.

  3. Vali Loki andmeallikaks.

  4. Sisesta LogQL päring süsteemi logide nägemiseks: 

    {job="varlogs"}

  5. Konfigureeri paneel:

  6. Title: System Logs
  7. Visualization: Vali Logs

  8. Kliki Apply

  9. Lisa paneel vealogide jaoks:

  10. Kliki Add new panel
  11. Vali Loki andmeallikaks
  12. Sisesta LogQL päring: 
    {job="varlogs"} |= "ERROR"
  13. Title: Error Logs
  14. Visualization: Vali Logs

  15. Kliki Apply

  16. Lisa paneel logide mahu jälgimiseks:

  17. Kliki Add new panel
  18. Vali Loki andmeallikaks
  19. Sisesta LogQL päring: 
    sum(count_over_time({job="varlogs"}[5m])) by (job)
  20. Title: Log Volume (5m intervals)
  21. Visualization: Vali Time series

  22. Kliki Apply

  23. Lisa paneel veamäära nägemiseks:

  24. Kliki Add new panel
  25. Vali Loki andmeallikaks
  26. Sisesta kaks päringut:
    • A: sum(count_over_time({job="varlogs"} |= "ERROR"[5m]))
    • B: sum(count_over_time({job="varlogs"}[5m]))
  27. Transform vahelehel lisa "Reduce" transformatsioon:
    • Mode: Binary operation
    • Operation: A/B (jagamine)
    • Multiply by: 100 (protsendi saamiseks)
  28. Title: Error Rate (%)
  29. Visualization: Vali Gauge

  30. Kliki Apply

  31. Salvesta dashboard:

  32. Kliki salvestamise ikooni (💾) üleval paremal
  33. Name: Log Analysis
  34. Folder: Application Monitoring
  35. Kliki Save

docs.title: 7. LogQL päringute loomine spetsiifiliste mustrite jaoks
docs.text:
LogQL on Loki päringukeel. Harjutame mõnede keerukamate päringute loomist:

  1. Lisa uus paneel oma Log Analysis dashboardi.

  2. Vali Loki andmeallikaks.

  3. Proovi järgmisi LogQL päringuid:

a. Filtreeri konkreetsete tekstimustrite järgi: 

{job="varlogs"} |= "connection" |= "timeout"

b. Loenda vigu aja jooksul: 

count_over_time({job="varlogs"} |= "ERROR"[1h])

c. Eraldage ja loendage veatüüpide järgi, kasutades regex mustrit: 

sum by (error_type) (count_over_time({job="varlogs"} |~ "ERROR: ([a-zA-Z ]+)" [1h]))

  1. Konfigureeri paneel:
  2. Title: Error Patterns
  3. Vali sobiv visualiseerimisviis vastavalt päringule

  4. Kliki Apply

  5. Salvesta dashboard.

docs.title: 8. Logide ja mõõdikute ühendamine
docs.text:
Tervikliku monitooringu võimsus seisneb logide ja mõõdikute ühendamises. Loome dashboardi, mis näitab seda:

  1. Navigeeri Dashboards → New Dashboard.

  2. Kliki Add new panel.

  3. Loo mitme paneeliga paigutus:

  4. CPU kasutamise graafik (Zabbixist)
  5. Süsteemi logid (Lokist)
  6. Veebi reageerimisaeg (Zabbixist)

  7. Veebi juurdepääsulogid (Lokist)

  8. Kasuta mall-muutujaid, et võimaldada filtreerimist hosti järgi:

  9. Kliki hammasratta ikoonil üleval paremal, et pääseda dashboardi seadeteni
  10. Vali "Variables" ja kliki "Add variable"
  11. Name: host
  12. Type: Query
  13. Data source: Zabbix
  14. Query type: Host

  15. Kliki Update

  16. Pane oma paneelid kasutama hosti muutujat, valides selle hosti rippmenüüst.

  17. Salvesta dashboard:

  18. Name: Unified Monitoring
  19. Folder: Infrastructure Monitoring
  20. Kliki Save

docs.title: 9.1 Dashboardi rotatsiooni seadistamine
docs.text:
NOC (Network Operations Center) ekraani jaoks võite seadistada automaatse dashboardide rotatsiooni:

  1. Installi Dashboard Carousel plugin: 

    docker-compose exec grafana grafana-cli plugins install smartmakers-trafficlight-panel
docker-compose restart grafana

  2. Navigeeri Dashboards → Playlists.

  3. Kliki New playlist.

  4. Sisesta üksikasjad:

  5. Name: Monitoring Overview
  6. Interval: 1m (1 minut)
  7. Vali oma dashboardid, mida kaasata

  8. Kliki Save

  9. Esitusloendi käivitamiseks kliki playlist ja seejärel Start playlist.

docs.title: 9.2 Dashboardi jagamise seadistamine
docs.text:
Seadistame meeskonnapääsu dashboardide jagamiseks:

  1. Navigeeri Configuration → Users.

  2. Kliki Invite, et lisada uus vaatajakasutaja.

  3. Sisesta e-posti aadress ja vali Viewer roll.

  4. Kliki Submit.

docs.title: 9.3 Kontrolli kogu monitooringusüsteemi
docs.text:
Veendume, et kõik komponendid töötavad koos:

  1. Navigeeri läbi kõigi oma dashboardide, et kontrollida, kas need näitavad andmeid.

  2. Genereeri mõned testsündmused: 

    # Genereeri CPU koormus
docker-compose exec zabbix-agent stress --cpu 2 --timeout 60

# Genereeri logisündmused
docker-compose exec zabbix-agent bash -c 'for i in {1..10}; do logger "WARNING: High CPU detected at $(date)"; sleep 1; done'

  3. Kontrolli, et:

  4. Mõõdikud Grafanas näitavad CPU tõusu
  5. Logid Lokis näitavad hoiatusteated

  6. Ühendatud dashboard näitab mõlemad koos

  7. Proovi andmete filtreerimist dashboard muutujate abil.

docs.title: 9.4 Tee nõutavad ekraanipildid esitamiseks
docs.text:
Tee järgmised ekraanipildid:

  1. Zabbix hosti konfiguratsiooniekraan koos elementide ja päästikutega
  2. Sinu süsteemi monitooringu dashboard Grafanas
  3. Logi analüüsimise dashboard, mis näitab mustreid ja korrelatsioone

docs.title: Kontrollnimekiri labori lõpetamiseks
docs.text:
• [ ] Docker Compose fail on korrektselt muudetud

docs.title: VirtualBox Setup Guide for Monitoring Lab
Resource Requirements
docs.text:
For optimal performance when running this monitoring lab in VirtualBox, configure your VM with:

  • CPU: 4 cores (or 2 cores)
  • RAM: 12-16GB ( alternative 8GB)
  • Storage: 50GB (dynamically allocated)
  • OS: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Server or Desktop
  • Network: Bridged Adapter (for easy access to web interfaces)

docs.title: Step-by-Step VirtualBox Setup
docs.text:
1. Install VirtualBox ( if you dont have it)
  2. Download and install from virtualbox.org

  3. Install the Extension Pack for better USB support and other features

  4. Create a New Virtual Machine

  5. Open VirtualBox and click "New"
  6. Name: Monitoring Lab
  7. Type: Linux
  8. Version: Ubuntu (64-bit)
  9. Follow the wizard, allocating resources as specified above
  10. Choose "Create a virtual hard disk now"
  11. Select "VDI (VirtualBox Disk Image)"
  12. Choose "Dynamically allocated" for storage

  13. Set size to 50GB

  14. Configure VM Settings

  15. Select your new VM and click "Settings"
  16. System → Processor: Set to 4 CPUs
  17. System → Motherboard: Enable EFI (if your host supports it)
  18. Display → Screen: Set Video Memory to 128MB
  19. Network → Adapter 1: Change to "Bridged Adapter"

  20. USB: Enable USB 3.0 controller

  21. Install Ubuntu

  22. Start the VM
  23. Select your Ubuntu ISO file when prompted
  24. Follow the Ubuntu installation process

  25. Choose "Install OpenSSH server" during setup for remote access

  26. Post-Installation Setup

  27. Install VirtualBox Guest Additions: 
    sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y build-essential linux-headers-$(uname -r)
  28. Insert Guest Additions CD from VirtualBox menu
  29. Mount and install: 
    sudo mount /dev/cdrom /mnt
cd /mnt
sudo ./VBoxLinuxAdditions.run

  30. Reboot the VM

  31. Take a Snapshot

  32. Once basic setup is complete, take a snapshot
  33. This allows you to return to a clean state if needed

docs.title: Troubleshooting Tips
docs.text:
• VM won't start with error about virtualization: Enable virtualization in your BIOS/UEFI
  • Performance issues: Reduce allocated resources or close other applications on host
  • Network problems: Try NAT with port forwarding if bridged adapter doesn't work
  • Shared folders not working: Reinstall Guest Additions and add user to vboxsf group

docs.title: Starting the Lab
docs.text: After VM setup: 1. Log in to your Ubuntu VM 2. Continue with Section 1.3 of the lab manual (Create Directory Structure)

docs.title: 🌟 Application Tracing Lab with Jaeger and OpenTelemetry
docs.text: You’ll run a simple application, generate trace logs, and learn about context propagation.

docs.title: 📚 Application Traces
docs.text:
Tracing (along with Metrics and Logs) forms the three pillars of observability: - Metrics → Health - Logs → Events - Traces → Communication flow

To trace, applications must emit spans and propagate context across services.

📖 References: - OpenTelemetry Specification - W3C Trace Context

docs.title: 🚀 Step 1: Run the Web Application
docs.text:
Start the web app: 

docker-compose -f labs/tracing/web.yml up -d
docker logs -f obsfun_fulfilment-web_1
Visit: http://localhost:8070

🛠️ You’ll see trace spans in logs:

Activity.Id: 00-<trace-id>-<span-id>-01
Activity.DisplayName: /
Activity.Kind: Server

📋 Checkpoint: What does this Activity represent?

Hint: It records HTTP request details like method, path, response time.

docs.title: 🛠️ Step 2: Trigger an Error
docs.text:
Click “Go” on the site. You’ll see:

❌ Documents service unavailable!

📋 Checkpoint: What caused the error?

Hint: The web app tries to call an API that isn’t running yet.

docs.title: 🚚 Step 3: Start the API Application
docs.text:
Start the API server: 

docker-compose -f labs/tracing/api.yml up -d
docker logs -f obsfun_fulfilment-api_1
Visit: http://localhost:8071/documents

✅ Now the web app can connect to the API.

docs.title: 🛜 Context Propagation
docs.text:
Every HTTP call carries the trace context using traceparent headers. - Clients send trace IDs. - Servers read and forward them.

This links all spans into a full distributed trace.

docs.title: 🧪 Step 4: Inject Your Own Trace ID
docs.text:
Use curl to inject a custom trace:

curl -H "traceparent: 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01" localhost:8070/index?all

Check the logs: 

docker logs obsfun_fulfilment-web_1 -n 20
docker logs obsfun_fulfilment-api_1 -n 10

📋 Checkpoint: Did both apps use your custom trace ID?

Hint: Parent span and child spans should have the same trace ID.

docs.title: 📜 W3C Trace Context Format
docs.text:
traceparent: 00-<trace-id>-<span-id>-<flags>

  • 00: version
  • trace-id: 16-byte hex ID
  • span-id: 8-byte hex ID
  • flags: 01 means sampled

🔗 Learn more

docs.title: 🧹 Cleanup
docs.text:
Remove all running containers:

docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq)

docs.title: 🎁 (Optional) Visualize with Jaeger
docs.text:
Create jaeger.yml: 

cat <<EOF > labs/tracing/jaeger.yml
version: '3.7'
services:
  jaeger:
    image: jaegertracing/all-in-one:latest
    ports:
      - "16686:16686"
      - "6831:6831/udp"
    networks:
      - fulfilment
networks:
  fulfilment:
    external: true
EOF
Start Jaeger: 
docker-compose -f labs/tracing/jaeger.yml up -d
Visit: http://localhost:16686

✅ View your traces in Jaeger UI!

docs.title: 🎯 Summary
docs.text: You learned: - How to run instrumented apps - How to view and understand traces - How context propagation connects services - How to inject traces manually - (Bonus) How to visualize traces in Jaeger

docs.title: 🏆 Congratulations!
docs.text:
You now understand Application Tracing with OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, and the W3C Trace Context!

🎉 Happy tracing!

docs.title: Lab 2: Distributed Tracing with Jaeger and OpenTelemetry
docs.text: In this lab, you'll set up Jaeger to collect and visualize traces from a sample application. You'll explore distributed tracing through Jaeger's web UI and investigate how spans are collected across multiple services.

docs.title: Step 1: Run Jaeger
docs.text:
We will start by launching a simple Jaeger instance where all components run in one container.

labs/jaeger/jaeger.yml 

version: '3.7'

services:
  jaeger:
    image: courselabs/jaeger:1.24
    ports:
      - "16686:16686"
    networks:
      - tracing  

networks:
  tracing:
    name: obsfun-tracing

Command: 

docker-compose -f labs/jaeger/jaeger.yml up -d

Open your browser and go to: 

http://localhost:16686

📋 Exercise 1: Select the jaeger-query service from the dropdown, click Find Traces, and open the first trace.

Jaeger records traces itself - you are seeing the call to the API from the web UI to list stored operations.
Tags like `http.method`, `http.status_code`, and `span.kind` give you useful metadata.
Switch to Trace Statistics or Trace JSON to see alternative data views.

docs.title: Step 2: Run the Application
docs.text:
The application has three components: - Web frontend - Document service API - Authorization service API

Configured to send spans to Jaeger via OpenTelemetry.

labs/jaeger/apps.yml 

version: '3.7'

services:

  fulfilment-api:
    image: courselabs/fulfilment-api
    ports:
      - "8071:80"
    environment:
      - OPENTRACING_JAEGER_ENABLED=true
    networks:
      - tracing 
      - fulfilment 

  fulfilment-authz:
    image: courselabs/fulfilment-authz
    ports:
      - "8072:80"
    environment:
      - Observability__Trace__Console=false
      - Observability__Trace__Jaeger=true
    networks:
      - tracing 
      - fulfilment 

  fulfilment-web:
    image: courselabs/fulfilment-web
    ports:
      - "8070:80"
    environment:
      - Observability__Trace__Console=false
      - Observability__Trace__Jaeger=true
      - Documents__Authz__Url=http://fulfilment-authz/check
    depends_on:
      - fulfilment-api
      - fulfilment-authz
    networks:
      - tracing 
      - fulfilment 

networks:
  fulfilment:
  tracing:
    name: obsfun-tracing

Command: 

docker-compose -f labs/jaeger/apps.yml up -d

Web app: 

http://localhost:8070

📋 Exercise 2: Open the trace for the homepage request to Fulfilment.Web.

There is likely just one span - a single request and response.
Traces with a single span are valid if no further calls happen.

docs.title: Step 3: Explore More Complex Traces
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the Document List page in the app.
  2. Click Go using default settings.

📋 Exercise 3: Find the trace for this interaction.

You'll now see multiple services involved!
Expand all spans:
- Web receives POST from user
- Web calls Authorization API (client+server spans)
- Authorization API makes an external GET request
- Web calls Document API (client+server spans)

Longest call is the external blog request.

docs.title: Step 4: Submit a Document
docs.text:
1. Go to the Submit Document page.
  2. Click Go.

📋 Exercise 4: Find the call stack for this request.

Trace call flow:
- POST /Submit (Web app)
- Web -> Authz (check permissions)
- Authz -> external site (identity check)
- Web -> Document API (submit document)

Find the final span (Document API POST) and check logs:
- handler.class_simple_name: DocumentsController
- handler.method_name: submitDocument

docs.title: 🛠 1. Setup: Start Services with Custom Spans
docs.text:
Use the provided compose.yml to launch the environment:

compose.yml

version: '3.7'

services:

  jaeger:
    image: courselabs/jaeger:1.24
    ports:
      - "16686:16686"
    networks:
      - tracing  

  fulfilment-api:
    image: courselabs/fulfilment-api
    ports:
      - "8071:80"
    environment:
      - OPENTRACING_JAEGER_ENABLED=true
      - TRACE_CUSTOM_SPANS=true
    networks:
      - tracing 
      - fulfilment 

  fulfilment-authz:
    image: courselabs/fulfilment-authz
    ports:
      - "8072:80"
    environment:
      - Observability__Trace__Console=false
      - Observability__Trace__Jaeger=true
    networks:
      - tracing 
      - fulfilment 

  fulfilment-web:
    image: courselabs/fulfilment-web
    ports:
      - "8070:80"
    environment:
      - Observability__Trace__Console=false
      - Observability__Trace__Jaeger=true
      - Documents__Authz__Url=http://fulfilment-authz/check
      - Observability__Trace__CustomSpans=true
    depends_on:
      - fulfilment-api
      - fulfilment-authz
    networks:
      - tracing 
      - fulfilment 

networks:
  fulfilment:
  tracing:
    name: obsfun-tracing

docs.title: ▶️ Start containers:
docs.text: docker-compose -f labs/custom-spans/compose.yml up -d

docs.title: 🌐 2. Access the Application
docs.text:
• Web app: http://localhost:8070
  • Jaeger UI: http://localhost:16686

Click Go on the web app to load the document list.

docs.title: 🔍 3. Explore Traces
docs.text:
In Jaeger UI: - Service: Fulfilment.Web - Operation: (Any) - Look for a trace with 10 spans.

You’ll find custom spans:

Span Name Notes list-documents Groups the entire request authz-check Around authorization call (tags: user ID, authz type, authz response) document-api-call Around document service call (tags: API action type)

docs.title: ✍️ 4. Custom Span Code Examples
docs.text:
C# (ListDocumentsService.cs) 👉 View on GitHub

apiSpan = _activitySource.StartActivity("document-api-call");
apiSpan.AddTag("span.kind", "internal")
       .AddTag("action.type", $"{DocumentAction.List}");

Java (DocumentsController.java) 👉 View on GitHub

dbLoadSpan = tracer.buildSpan("database-load").start();
dbLoadSpan.setTag("span.kind", "internal");

Both examples use: - try/finally to ensure spans close properly even on errors.

docs.title: 🧠 5. Find Problems Using Tags
docs.text:
Change the User ID to 1042 in the web app. Click Go.

You will get a Documents service unavailable error.

In Jaeger UI:

  1. Search Service: Fulfilment.Web
  2. Add tag: 
    user.id = 1042
  3. Find the trace.

You’ll see: - AuthZ span shows a denied authorization tag.

docs.title: 🛠 6. Setup Baggage for Full Trace Context
docs.text:
Update with baggage support:

update.yml

version: '3.7'

services:

  fulfilment-api:
    image: courselabs/fulfilment-api
    ports:
      - "8071:80"
    environment:
      - OPENTRACING_JAEGER_ENABLED=true
      - TRACE_CUSTOM_SPANS=true
      - TRACE_BAGGAGE_TAG=true
    networks:
      - tracing 
      - fulfilment 

  fulfilment-authz:
    image: courselabs/fulfilment-authz
    ports:
      - "8072:80"
    environment:
      - Observability__Trace__Console=false
      - Observability__Trace__Jaeger=true
      - Observability__Trace__Baggage__Tag=true
    networks:
      - tracing 
      - fulfilment 

  fulfilment-web:
    image: courselabs/fulfilment-web
    ports:
      - "8070:80"
    environment:
      - Observability__Trace__Console=false
      - Observability__Trace__Jaeger=true
      - Documents__Authz__Url=http://fulfilment-authz/check
      - Observability__Trace__CustomSpans=true
      - Observability__Trace__Baggage__Tag=true
    depends_on:
      - fulfilment-authz
    networks:
      - tracing 
      - fulfilment 

networks:
  fulfilment:
  tracing:
    name: obsfun-tracing

▶️ Update containers:

docker-compose -f labs/custom-spans/update.yml up -d

docs.title: 🧩 7. Explore Traces with Baggage
docs.text:
Browse the document list page again (user 0421).

In Jaeger, you’ll now see transaction.id attached (copied as a tag from baggage)!

docs.title: ✨ 8. BONUS: Skipping Authorization Using Baggage
docs.text:
Use a curl command to force skip authorization:

curl -H "baggage: authz.skip=true" "http://localhost:8070/index?userId=1024"
  • You’ll successfully get the documents even though normally user 1024 is unauthorized.
  • The authz-check span in Jaeger will show authorization skipped.

docs.title: 📄 Summary: Key Concepts
docs.text: Feature Use Custom Spans Group related operations, add logical visibility Tags Add searchable context to spans Baggage Attach metadata that travels through call chains (headers) Skipping Authorization Dangerous but possible via baggage manipulation

docs.title: 📊 Lab: End-to-End Monitoring with Prometheus, Grafana, and PagerDuty
docs.text:
Welcome! In this lab, you’ll learn how to monitor a system using: - Prometheus for collecting metrics - Grafana for creating dashboards - PagerDuty for sending alerts

Based on the GitHub project: 🔗 https://github.com/ibraheemcisse/End-to-End-Monitoring-Setup-Prometheus-Grafana-and-PagerDuty

docs.title: 🖥️ Step 0: Prepare Your Virtual Machine (VM)
docs.text:
Before starting the lab, create a Linux VM with the following specs:

  • OS: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (preferred) or Debian-based
  • CPU: 2 cores minimum
  • RAM: 2 GB (4 GB recommended)
  • Disk: 10+ GB
  • Network: Must have internet access
  • Pre-installed tools: wget, tar, curl, nano, systemctl

docs.title: Recommended Platforms:
docs.text:
• Local: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation Player
  • Cloud: AWS EC2 (t2.micro), Google Cloud (e2-micro), Azure (B1s)

🔐 If using cloud, open ports 3000 and 9090 to access Grafana and Prometheus.

docs.title: ⚠️ Network & Access Tips
docs.text:
• Local VM: Use http://localhost:9090 and http://localhost:3000
  • Cloud VM: Use http://<your-vm-ip>:9090 and http://<your-vm-ip>:3000
  • Open these ports in your cloud firewall settings.
  • ✅ PagerDuty works without needing public URLs — alerts are sent outbound.

docs.title: 📁 Step 1: Clone the Project
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/ibraheemcisse/End-to-End-Monitoring-Setup-Prometheus-Grafana-and-PagerDuty.git
cd End-to-End-Monitoring-Setup-Prometheus-Grafana-and-PagerDuty

docs.title: 📦 Step 2: Install Prometheus
docs.text:
wget https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/releases/latest/download/prometheus-*.linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar -xvzf prometheus-*.linux-amd64.tar.gz
cd prometheus-*.linux-amd64/

Edit prometheus.yml:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'node_exporter'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9100']

Run Prometheus:

./prometheus --config.file=prometheus.yml

Visit http://localhost:9090

docs.title: 📊 Step 3: Install Grafana
docs.text:
wget https://dl.grafana.com/oss/release/grafana-10.0.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar -zxvf grafana-10.0.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz
cd grafana-10.0.0/
./bin/grafana-server

Visit http://localhost:3000 — login: admin/admin

docs.title: 🔌 Step 4: Connect Grafana to Prometheus
docs.text:
1. Settings > Data Sources > Add Data Source
  2. Choose Prometheus
  3. URL: http://localhost:9090 (or cloud IP)
  4. Click Save & Test

docs.title: 🧭 Step 5: Create Dashboards
docs.text:
Create → Dashboard → Add panel

CPU Query: 

100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100)

Memory Query: 

(1 - (node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes)) * 100

Disk Query: 

100 - ((node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"}) * 100)

docs.title: What is PagerDuty?
docs.text: PagerDuty is a real-time incident response platform used by IT teams to detect, escalate, and resolve issues rapidly. Founded in 2009, it has become a standard in DevOps, SRE, and IT Operations. Trusted by thousands of companies, it integrates with tools like Grafana, Slack, AWS, and more.

docs.title: Create a PagerDuty Service
docs.text:
1. Sign up at https://www.pagerduty.com
  2. Go to Services > + New Service
  3. Integration Type: Events API v2
  4. Copy the Integration Key

docs.title: 📢 Step 7: Connect PagerDuty to Grafana
docs.text:
1. Grafana > Alerting > Notification Channels > Add Channel
  2. Type: PagerDuty
  3. Paste the Integration Key
  4. Name: PagerDuty Alerts
  5. Save

docs.title: ⚙️ Step 8: Create Alert Rule
docs.text:
Grafana > Alerting > Alert Rules > + Create

Query:

100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100)

Condition: last value > 90 for 1 minute → Notify: PagerDuty Alerts

docs.title: 🧪 Step 9: Test Alerts
docs.text:
1. Use "Test Rule" in Grafana
  2. Simulate high CPU or edit value temporarily
  3. Check PagerDuty dashboard for alert

docs.title: 🧪 Step 10: Test the Alert Delivery (Get Email/SMS/Call)
✅ Before You Start
docs.text: Make sure: - You created a PagerDuty user account - You added your email and phone number under User Settings - Your notification rules are set (e.g., "SMS immediately", "Call me after 1 min")

docs.title: 🧪 Option A: Simulate CPU Spike (Real)
docs.text:
Run this in your VM:

yes > /dev/null &

This will use 100% CPU and trigger the alert. To stop it, run:

killall yes

docs.title: 🧪 Option B: Use Grafana Test Button (Quick)
docs.text:
1. Go to Alerting > Alert Rules
  2. Click the rule (e.g., "High CPU")
  3. Click Test Rule
  4. You should receive an alert via email, SMS, or call

docs.title: 📱 Optional: Use the PagerDuty Mobile App
docs.text:
• Install from your app store
  • Log in and allow push notifications

docs.title: 🧹 Step 11: Clean Up (Prevent Billing!)
docs.text:
PagerDuty trial accounts may convert to paid if not canceled. To avoid charges:

  1. Go to your PagerDuty account settings
  2. Cancel/delete the account before your trial ends
  3. Or downgrade to the free tier (if available)

⚠️ Failure to cancel may result in unexpected billing after the trial period.

docs.text: ✅ Metrics collected with Prometheus ✅ Dashboards created with Grafana ✅ Alerts delivered using PagerDuty

docs.title: 🔍 Introduction to Elasticsearch
docs.text: Welcome to your first steps with Elasticsearch – the powerful engine behind modern search and analytics. By the end of this guide, you’ll know what Elasticsearch does, how it works, and why companies like Netflix and Uber rely on it every day.

docs.title: 📘 1. What is Elasticsearch?
docs.text: Elasticsearch is like Google, but for your data. It’s a super-fast, scalable search engine that helps you find and analyze information almost instantly.

docs.title: 🚀 The Origin Story
docs.text:
• Created by Shay Banon in 2010
  • Started as a project to help his wife search through recipes
  • Now powers giants like Netflix, LinkedIn, and Uber

docs.title: 🧠 What It Can Do
docs.text:
• Store & search terabytes of data
  • Handle text, numbers, locations, dates, and more
  • Provide lightning-fast search and filtering

🔗 Official Site

docs.title: 🧾 2. What is JSON?
docs.text:
Before diving deeper, meet JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) — the language of Elasticsearch.

Here’s an example:

{
  "name": "John Smith",
  "age": 35,
  "email": "john@example.com",
  "interests": ["hiking", "cooking", "photography"]
}
````

🧩 **Why it matters**: JSON makes it easy to describe data using **key-value pairs**. Elasticsearch speaks JSON fluently.

---

## 🧱 3. Elasticsearch Architecture

![Architecture](https://dz2cdn1.dzone.com/storage/temp/16817828-1680796576192.png)

### 🖥️ What’s a Cluster?

A **cluster** is a team of computers (called **nodes**) working together.

| Scenario    | Description                   |
| ----------- | ----------------------------- |
| Single Node | One person doing all the work |
| Cluster     | A team sharing the workload   |

✅ **Benefits of clustering**:

* Scales up with your data
* Searches in parallel = speed boost
* Redundant = more reliable

![Cluster Node Diagram](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize\:fit:720/format\:webp/1*rfcn4XSrNI1KZFbq89l7Jw.png)

---

## 📚 4. Key Concepts

![Components](https://softjourn.com/media/images/Articles/Elasticsearch101/Elasticsearch101-Picture_\(8\).png)

### 📄 Document

A document = one unit of data (e.g., a recipe, user profile, or book).

```json
{
  "title": "The Great Gatsby",
  "author": "F. Scott Fitzgerald",
  "year": 1925,
  "genres": ["Novel", "Fiction", "Classic"]
}

docs.title: 📁 Index
docs.text:
A collection of related documents, like a database table.

➡️ Powered by Apache Lucene’s inverted index:

docs.title: 🧩 Shards & Replicas
docs.text:
Term Description Shard A piece of an index – spreads data across nodes Replica A copy of a shard – provides backup and faster access

📘 Analogy:

  • Shards = book chapters read by multiple people
  • Replicas = photocopies for safety and speed

docs.title: 🧰 5. The Elastic Stack (a.k.a. ELK Stack)
docs.text:
Elasticsearch is part of a powerful toolkit:

Tool Role Elasticsearch Stores & searches your data Kibana Visualizes the data (charts, dashboards) Logstash Processes and transforms incoming data Beats Lightweight agents that send data into the stack

📦 Together, they form the ELK Stack.

docs.title: 🔧 6. Basic Elasticsearch Operations
docs.text: Elasticsearch uses RESTful HTTP APIs to interact with data.

docs.title: 🆕 Create an Index
docs.text:
PUT /books
{
  "settings": {
    "number_of_shards": 3,
    "number_of_replicas": 1
  }
}

{
  "title": "Pride and Prejudice",
  "author": "Jane Austen",
  "year": 1813,
  "genres": ["Romance", "Classic"]

docs.title: 🔍 Search for a Document
docs.text:
GET /books/_search
{
  "query": {
    "match": {
      "author": "austen"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: 👥 Who’s Using Elasticsearch?
docs.text:
• Netflix – 1.5+ trillion events per day
  • GitHub – Search for code, issues, PRs
  • Uber – Maps, locations, and rides
  • Wikipedia – Full-text search
  • Walmart – Inventory in real time
  • Goldman Sachs – Instant risk analysis

docs.text:
1. Real-time log aggregation
  2. Time-series metrics collection
  3. Instant alerts for anomalies
  4. Designed for huge, distributed systems
  5. Beautiful, live visual dashboards

docs.title: 🆚 Bonus: Elasticsearch vs. OpenSearch
docs.text:
OpenSearch is a fork of Elasticsearch created by Amazon.

🧠 Wrap-up: Elasticsearch turns data into insights. Whether you’re building a search engine, monitoring logs, or analyzing trends—this tool is a game-changer.

📣 “Just like Google helps you search the web, Elasticsearch helps you search your world.”

docs.title: 📚 Introduction
docs.text: ElasticSearch operates on a RESTful interface, making it accessible through standard HTTP requests. This modern architecture ensures scalability, flexibility, and language-agnostic integration capabilities.

docs.title: 🌟 Key Benefits

• Language-agnostic implementation
  • Scalable and distributed architecture

docs.title: 🔄 HTTP Request/Response Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant ES as ElasticSearch Server

    Note over C,ES: HTTP Request Components
    C->>+ES: HTTP Request
    Note right of C: 1. Method (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE)<br/>2. Protocol (HTTP/1.1)<br/>3. Host (domain)<br/>4. URL (path)<br/>5. Headers<br/>6. Request Body
    ES-->>-C: HTTP Response
    Note left of ES: 1. Status Code<br/>2. Response Headers<br/>3. Response Body (JSON)

docs.text: Elastic Stack is an open-source collection of tools for data analysis, processing, storage, and visualization. It is known as the ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), which also includes Beats.

docs.title: Kibana – data visualization
docs.text: Kibana provides pie charts, line charts, histograms, and maps. It can visualize Elasticsearch data and format it as desired.

docs.text:

Introduction to Elasticsearch Architecture

docs.text:
Beats are lightweight agents that send data from machines to Logstash or directly to Elasticsearch. For example: Filebeat monitors log files and imports them.

Elastic Stack centralizes data and provides powerful tools for analysis and visualization.
